REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] The claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, file number MB7-08411, is a citizen of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). He has claimed refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
DETERMINATION

[2] The Tribunal finds that the claimant has not established a well-founded fear of persecution based on a Convention ground. The Tribunal also finds that the claimant has not demonstrated, on the balance of probabilities, that he is a "person in need of protection".
THE CLAIMANT'S ALLEGATIONS

[3] The claimant is a XXXX XXXX XXXX year-old male from the city of Lubumbashi. He fears for his life because the authorities perceived him to be an opponent of the government.

[4] Since 2005, the claimant has been a member of the Église Ministère de la Restauration à partir de l'Afrique Noire. The leader of the church, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a politician who has denounced the regime of President Joseph Kabila. As a result, Congo's National Intelligence Agency (ANR) would send agents to monitors the church's activities.

[5] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013, the authorities arrested members of the church who had been distributing a letter from XXXX. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013, soldiers came to the church looking for XXXX, but he was not present. A confrontation occurred during which a member of the church died.

[6] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013, members of the church organized a protest against the arrest of their fellow members. In response, the government got armed troops to attack the state TV station, the international airport and a military base. The authorities then blamed the claimant's church for the attacks, forcing XXXX to flee to South Africa.

[7] The government began by arresting only senior members of the church such that the claimant was not initially afraid. However, in XXXX 2014, the claimant learned that regular members were also being arrested. He therefore fled to the home of his brother in the city of Likasi.

[8] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, the authorities arrested the claimant and asked him questions about the church's plans. The government mistreated the claimant and proceeded to detain him until XXXX XXXX, 2014. On that date, the claimant's uncle arranged for his escape from the prison where he was being held.

[9] The claimant returned to his brother's home in Likasi, but was again arrested on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. The authorities asked the claimant questions about XXXX plans against the government. The claimant's uncle arranged for his second escape from prison on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015.

[10] After leaving detention, the claimant hid in a remote village where he found life extremely difficult. His uncle began efforts to arrange for the claimant's departure from the DRC. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, the claimant travelled to Zambia to attend an interview at the American embassy.

[11] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, the claimant left the DRC to attend a church conference along with the Nouvelle City de David church. Once in the United States, the claimant travelled to Canada because his sister was living here. On XXXX 2016, he claimed refugee status at a border entry point.
ANALYSIS
The Claimant has Sufficiently Established his Identity

subthemes.text:
[12] The Tribunal must take into account whether claimants possess acceptable documentation establishing their identity.1 In the present case, the claimant has submitted a passport from the RDC which contains a visa to the United States.2 These documents are sufficient to establish the claimant's identity for the purposes of claiming refugee status in Canada.
The Claimant's Allegations Are Not Credible

[13] When providing testimony under oath, refugee claimants benefit from a presumption that their allegations are true.3 In the present case, however, the Tribunal finds serious reasons for rejecting the claimant's testimony based on its lack of credibility.

[14] In his written narrative, the claimant states that he was a member of the Ministère de la Restauration à partir de l'Afrique Noire. Congolese authorities blamed this church for the events of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013 and the church leader fled to South Africa. In XXXX 2014, the claimant would have fled to the home of his brother because all church members were then facing arrest.

[15] During the hearing, the Tribunal asked the claimant why he did not flee to his brother's home immediately after the XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013 incidents. Consistent with his written narrative, the claimant explained that the authorities were initially interested only in church executives. The Tribunal then asked the claimant how he could have been certain that the authorities would not arrest him, a simple member. The claimant explained that it had not been a secret that Congolese authorities had initially wanted only senior church members.

[16] Later in the hearing, counsel for the claimant asked him where he had learned that only church executives had faced arrest. The claimant replied that information was leaking all of the time, and he referred to Zambia. Asked who had personally revealed this information to him, the claimant said that he got it from his brother.

[17] The Tribunal finds that the claimant has not provided reasonable explanations for his actions following the events of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013. Documentary evidence submitted by the claimant indicates that the Congolese authorities' immediate response to these events was widespread. Moreover, the authorities were seeking any person identified as being a member of Ministère de la Restauration à partir de l'Afrique Noire.4

[18] As a member of this church, the claimant would reasonably have be aware of the authorities' reaction which received extensive media coverage.5 The Tribunal finds it unreasonable that the claimant would have then relied on information from his brother indicating that he had not initially faced arrest. In the Tribunal's view, the claimant delay in fleeing after XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013 damages his credibility in regards to the threat that he allegedly faces.

[19] In his written narrative, the claimant states that the ANR arrested him at his parents' home on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. In their offices, the ANR would have physically mistreated the claimant and then sent him to detention in a jail. The claimant further testified that he escaped from the jail on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014 with the help of his uncle.

[20] The Tribunal asked the claimant why, after his escape from jail, he would have fled to the home of his brother. The claimant explained that he had been arrested in Lubumbashi but that his brother lived in Likasi. Asked why he had thought that the ANR could not find him at his brother's home, the claimant added that his uncle had told him to go to Likasi.

[21] In light of his other allegations, the Tribunal finds that the claimant has not provided a reasonable explanation. In his written narrative, the claimant states that, prior to his arrest, he had hid at his brother's home for a month. The claimant would have then moved to his parents' home because he was afraid of staying too long in one place.

subthemes.text:
[22] In the Tribunal's view the claimant had allegedly been aware of the risk of staying at his brother's home. The Tribunal could reasonably have expected him to have made other arrangements, as his did after his second arrest. The Tribunal finds that the claimant's credibility to be damaged in regards to whether the ANR arrested him.

[23] In his written narrative, the claimant states that the ARN arrested him a second time on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. The claimant would have succeeded in escaping the jail, once again with the help of his uncle. The claimant states that he then stayed in a remote village until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, when he travelled to Zambia to obtain a U.S. visa.

[24] The Tribunal asked the claimant to explain why he returned to the RDC after his interview at the U.S. embassy. The claimant explained that he was planning to travel with a group and that he had had no choice. The claimant also stated that his uncle had instructed him to stay in Lubumbashi where the uncle could provide some security.

[25] The Tribunal then confronted the claimant with content of the documentary evidence which he provided. The available sources indicate that many members of the claimant's church organization had fled to Zambia.6 In response, the claimant simply reiterated that he had been following the instructions of his uncle.

[26] The Tribunal finds that the claimant has not provided a reasonable explanation for his re-availment of the RDC. The claimant has provided no reason why he could not have remained in Zambia, except to follow his uncle's instruction for travel to the U.S. In the Tribunal's view, the claimant's behaviour is not compatible with that of the person fearing persecution. The Tribunal finds the claimant's credibility further damaged with regards to whether Congolese authorities have sought him.

[27] In support of his allegations, the claimant has submitted a letter from the Centre international de formation en droits humains et développement.7 This letter indicates that ANR detained the claimant for political reasons. However, the letter writer does not explain how he obtained first-hand knowledge of this alleged incident. Consequently, the Tribunal finds that this letter has insufficient probative value to re-establish the claimant's credibility.

[28] The claimant has also provided various documents pertaining to his brother's successful claim for refugee status in South Africa.8 However, the documents in question provide little information about the basis of the brother's refugee claim. Therefore, the Tribunal is unable to determine whether the facts of that case correspond with the allegations of the claimant. On this basis, the Tribunal finds that these documents also lack sufficient probative value to re-establish the claimant's credibility.

[29] Finally, to support his allegations, the claimant has submitted a series of e-mails between himself and family members.9 However, in each case, the claimant initiated the e-mails exchanges after he had claimed refugee status in Canada. The Tribunal finds that the content of these emails is therefore insufficient to re-establish the claimant's credibility.

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] The claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, file number MB7-08411, is a citizen of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). He has claimed refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
DETERMINATION

[2] The Tribunal finds that the claimant has not established a well-founded fear of persecution based on a Convention ground. The Tribunal also finds that the claimant has not demonstrated, on the balance of probabilities, that he is a "person in need of protection".
THE CLAIMANT'S ALLEGATIONS
[3] The claimant is a XXXX XXXX XXXX year-old male from the city of Lubumbashi. He fears for his life because the authorities perceived him to be an opponent of the government.

[4] Since 2005, the claimant has been a member of the Église Ministère de la Restauration à partir de l'Afrique Noire. The leader of the church, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a politician who has denounced the regime of President Joseph Kabila. As a result, Congo's National Intelligence Agency (ANR) would send agents to monitors the church's activities.

[5] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013, the authorities arrested members of the church who had been distributing a letter from XXXX. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013, soldiers came to the church looking for XXXX, but he was not present. A confrontation occurred during which a member of the church died.

[6] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013, members of the church organized a protest against the arrest of their fellow members. In response, the government got armed troops to attack the state TV station, the international airport and a military base. The authorities then blamed the claimant's church for the attacks, forcing XXXX to flee to South Africa.

[7] The government began by arresting only senior members of the church such that the claimant was not initially afraid. However, in XXXX 2014, the claimant learned that regular members were also being arrested. He therefore fled to the home of his brother in the city of Likasi.

[8] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, the authorities arrested the claimant and asked him questions about the church's plans. The government mistreated the claimant and proceeded to detain him until XXXX XXXX, 2014. On that date, the claimant's uncle arranged for his escape from the prison where he was being held.

[9] The claimant returned to his brother's home in Likasi, but was again arrested on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. The authorities asked the claimant questions about XXXX plans against the government. The claimant's uncle arranged for his second escape from prison on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015.

[10] After leaving detention, the claimant hid in a remote village where he found life extremely difficult. His uncle began efforts to arrange for the claimant's departure from the DRC. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, the claimant travelled to Zambia to attend an interview at the American embassy.

[11] On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, the claimant left the DRC to attend a church conference along with the Nouvelle City de David church. Once in the United States, the claimant travelled to Canada because his sister was living here. On XXXX 2016, he claimed refugee status at a border entry point.
ANALYSIS
The Claimant has Sufficiently Established his Identity

[12] The Tribunal must take into account whether claimants possess acceptable documentation establishing their identity.1 In the present case, the claimant has submitted a passport from the RDC which contains a visa to the United States.2 These documents are sufficient to establish the claimant's identity for the purposes of claiming refugee status in Canada.
The Claimant's Allegations Are Not Credible

[13] When providing testimony under oath, refugee claimants benefit from a presumption that their allegations are true.3 In the present case, however, the Tribunal finds serious reasons for rejecting the claimant's testimony based on its lack of credibility.

[14] In his written narrative, the claimant states that he was a member of the Ministère de la Restauration à partir de l'Afrique Noire. Congolese authorities blamed this church for the events of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013 and the church leader fled to South Africa. In XXXX 2014, the claimant would have fled to the home of his brother because all church members were then facing arrest.

[15] During the hearing, the Tribunal asked the claimant why he did not flee to his brother's home immediately after the XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013 incidents. Consistent with his written narrative, the claimant explained that the authorities were initially interested only in church executives. The Tribunal then asked the claimant how he could have been certain that the authorities would not arrest him, a simple member. The claimant explained that it had not been a secret that Congolese authorities had initially wanted only senior church members.

[16] Later in the hearing, counsel for the claimant asked him where he had learned that only church executives had faced arrest. The claimant replied that information was leaking all of the time, and he referred to Zambia. Asked who had personally revealed this information to him, the claimant said that he got it from his brother.

[17] The Tribunal finds that the claimant has not provided reasonable explanations for his actions following the events of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013. Documentary evidence submitted by the claimant indicates that the Congolese authorities' immediate response to these events was widespread. Moreover, the authorities were seeking any person identified as being a member of Ministère de la Restauration à partir de l'Afrique Noire.4

[18] As a member of this church, the claimant would reasonably have be aware of the authorities' reaction which received extensive media coverage.5 The Tribunal finds it unreasonable that the claimant would have then relied on information from his brother indicating that he had not initially faced arrest. In the Tribunal's view, the claimant delay in fleeing after XXXX XXXX XXXX 2013 damages his credibility in regards to the threat that he allegedly faces.

[19] In his written narrative, the claimant states that the ANR arrested him at his parents' home on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. In their offices, the ANR would have physically mistreated the claimant and then sent him to detention in a jail. The claimant further testified that he escaped from the jail on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014 with the help of his uncle.

[20] The Tribunal asked the claimant why, after his escape from jail, he would have fled to the home of his brother. The claimant explained that he had been arrested in Lubumbashi but that his brother lived in Likasi. Asked why he had thought that the ANR could not find him at his brother's home, the claimant added that his uncle had told him to go to Likasi.

[21] In light of his other allegations, the Tribunal finds that the claimant has not provided a reasonable explanation. In his written narrative, the claimant states that, prior to his arrest, he had hid at his brother's home for a month. The claimant would have then moved to his parents' home because he was afraid of staying too long in one place.

[22] In the Tribunal's view the claimant had allegedly been aware of the risk of staying at his brother's home. The Tribunal could reasonably have expected him to have made other arrangements, as his did after his second arrest. The Tribunal finds that the claimant's credibility to be damaged in regards to whether the ANR arrested him.

[23] In his written narrative, the claimant states that the ARN arrested him a second time on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014. The claimant would have succeeded in escaping the jail, once again with the help of his uncle. The claimant states that he then stayed in a remote village until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, when he travelled to Zambia to obtain a U.S. visa.

[24] The Tribunal asked the claimant to explain why he returned to the RDC after his interview at the U.S. embassy. The claimant explained that he was planning to travel with a group and that he had had no choice. The claimant also stated that his uncle had instructed him to stay in Lubumbashi where the uncle could provide some security.

[25] The Tribunal then confronted the claimant with content of the documentary evidence which he provided. The available sources indicate that many members of the claimant's church organization had fled to Zambia.6 In response, the claimant simply reiterated that he had been following the instructions of his uncle.

[26] The Tribunal finds that the claimant has not provided a reasonable explanation for his re-availment of the RDC. The claimant has provided no reason why he could not have remained in Zambia, except to follow his uncle's instruction for travel to the U.S. In the Tribunal's view, the claimant's behaviour is not compatible with that of the person fearing persecution. The Tribunal finds the claimant's credibility further damaged with regards to whether Congolese authorities have sought him.

[27] In support of his allegations, the claimant has submitted a letter from the Centre international de formation en droits humains et développement.7 This letter indicates that ANR detained the claimant for political reasons. However, the letter writer does not explain how he obtained first-hand knowledge of this alleged incident. Consequently, the Tribunal finds that this letter has insufficient probative value to re-establish the claimant's credibility.

[28] The claimant has also provided various documents pertaining to his brother's successful claim for refugee status in South Africa.8 However, the documents in question provide little information about the basis of the brother's refugee claim. Therefore, the Tribunal is unable to determine whether the facts of that case correspond with the allegations of the claimant. On this basis, the Tribunal finds that these documents also lack sufficient probative value to re-establish the claimant's credibility.

[29] Finally, to support his allegations, the claimant has submitted a series of e-mails between himself and family members.9 However, in each case, the claimant initiated the e-mails exchanges after he had claimed refugee status in Canada. The Tribunal finds that the content of these emails is therefore insufficient to re-establish the claimant's credibility.

[30] For these reasons, the Tribunal finds that the claimant has not provided credible testimony. The Tribunal concludes that the claimant has not established his allegations on the balance of probabilities.
CONCLUSION

[31] The Tribunal concludes that the claimant has not demonstrated a serious possibility of being the subject of persecution as per section 96 of the IRPA. He has also not established, on a balance of probabilities, a danger of torture, a threat to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment (section 97(1) of the IRPA).
DECISION

[32] The claim is denied.
